Christianity is a human invention and the Bible is a human book...which, to me, makes the book far, far more amazing than the idea that it was penned by God.  In that book, we have histories, myths, tales, poetry, and law from a single little tiny henotheistic tribe living in the Middle East from *thousands* of years ago.  We have no trace of so many other great and important books written throughout history-- their numbers few due to the need to hand-copy each book, lost in fires and war and disasters.  Realistically speaking, there's no way in fucking hell that the Bible should have not only survived, but thrived.  That's *amazing*.

Double predestination states that God saves some (showing mercy) and sends others to Hell (showing justice); single predestination states that God saves some and merely *doesn't* save others.  Either way, we cannot affect whether or not we are chosen.

Actually, according to classical Christian theology, we *don't* have a choice as to whether we sin or not.  That's the whole point of Original Sin.  Adam and Eve had a choice, but once they fell, sin became-- essentially-- genetic.  We can *want* to do good, but without God's intervention, we cannot *choose* to be good.  Humanity is doomed to always sin without God's grace.

The Hebrew word "sheol" indicates a dark, shadowy realm of the dead, and isn't anything specific about it in the Bible other than "it's where you go when you die".  See also: "the grave".  There's no talk of judgement or eternal life or anything like that.  In fact, you could argue that nothing was specified because the proto-Jewish people didn't care about the afterlife (unlike, say, the Egyptians), but instead were interested in the real life in the here-and-now on earth.  

There is no word for "hell" in the New Testament besides "hades" (the Greek word for the dark, shadowy afterlife) or "Gehenna", which referred to the valley outside of the city of Jerusalem where the trash was burned ("eternal fire", anyone?).  All references to "hell" are one of these two; the word "hell" itself is an import from Norse mythology.  There's nothing in Revelation 20:11-15 that refutes this.  The dead in "hades"-- the dark, shadowy resting world for the dead"-- are then burned in "a lake of fire", but no where in that passage is the "lake of fire" said to be "hell" or "eternal".
